Benny & the Fossils

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
For almost 5 decades, Benny Mbotho has been the custodian of the earliest Upper Cretaceous fossil deposit known...

Unique Selling Point:
Benny Mbotho grew up on the Wild Coast, playing amongst the fossil beds on the coastline. And since he learned their value at the age of nine, he has been safeguarding them, and is the local tour guide for the Mzamba Petrified Forest and fossil beds.

When Mbotho went to the beach as a child, he didn’t realise he was walking on the sands of history. At the age of nine, playing drums on the rocks, an older friend told him he was in fact sitting on the fossilised shell of a long-gone sea turtle. Mbotho looked around him, and saw that there was an entire world to be discovered right in front of him, from remnants of shark teeth to giant clams. Known as the Petrified Forest, the beach is also littered with fossilised trees washed down from the land. After witnessing geologists examine the area, Mbotho took it upon himself to research the coast and its gems.

Summary:
We visit the Mzamba Petrified Forest and Fossil beds and meet the self-appointed custodian, Benny Mbotho. Benny is a self-taught expert on the wide variety of fossils that can be found on this 1km stretch of beach just around the corner from the Wild Coast Sun. The Mzamba Fossil Bed is the earliest Upper Cretaceous fossil deposit known -- The Formation gives a compacted record of the era between 80 and 86 million years ago, with fossils of 1 metre mussels, shark teeth, petrified trees and even a strelitzia.

For Benny it is imperative that this natural heritage is preserved and he loves teaching visitors about the site and the fossils.

Further information:
The Mzamba fossils and Petrified Forest are on the beach, about 2 km from the Wild Coast Sun, near Port Edward, in the northerly reaches of the Wild Coast.

You'll find the Petrified Forest - a series of marine fossil beds, which are actually fossilised logs embedded in rocks - exposed in a series of prominent reefs just south of the Mtamvuna River, passed Thompson's lagoon. The wood was once part of a forest, carried downstream by rivers and waterlogged here in the shallows of the coast.

These are sandstone and limestone deposits containing fossils that date back 80 million years to the Upper Cretaceous period, and include marine shells, bivalve shells, coiled ammonites, echinoids (or sea urchins) and, incredibly, a fossilised sea turtle and enormous clam shells.

White Man's Cave is a fossilised overhang. You can sit beneath it and study a series of further fossils from below. The forest and the fossils are collectively known as the Mzamba Cretaceous Deposits.

Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Port Edward/ Wild Coast Sun
Accommodation
3 people

Script:


BENNY AND THE FOSSILS




Benny
I always dream about these fossils. And every time I come on the beach is like my first day…



Upsound
VO
These fossilised tree trunks have been lying here beneath the waves since the age of the dinosaurs, over 80 million years ago. They form part of a unique fossil formation – the earliest Upper Cretaceous deposits known to man.


And for almost half a century Benny Mbotho has been the guardian of these fossils…
LINK
80 million years ago earth was a very different place. The climate was warmer and dense tropical forests covered large parts of the planet – even at the polar caps… These waters were inhabited by giant clams and ammonites… And the Mzamba fossil beds give us a glimpse into the world…


Our story of Benny and the Fossils starts early on a Monday morning as we make our way to a small coastal village, just a stone’s throw away from the KwaZulu-Natal / Eastern Cape border…
Benny
I was born here and I grew up in a couple of places around South Africa, like Durban, Eastern Cape and Cape Town… but I was always dreaming about this little village of mine…




VO
We arrive just in time for breakfast…
Benny
Benny: Goats are one of the traditional animals. That is why I like to keep them. And I don’t slaughter them, but I know even when I’m with the goats here in my house my ancestors are happy. You can slaughter a cow, maybe 5 cows, for your event, but if you forgot to bring the goat first, it doesn't work out.

Claire: Absolutely. Does your wife like the goats?

Benny: She loves them.

Claire: Okay.


VO
Benny is an electrician and musician, but his real passion is for the natural environment, sharing his knowledge and experiences with everyone… from tourists to learners in the local schools…
Benny
It’s all about teaching the children how to look after some environmental things that are very important to us, like trees and stuff. Because we black people, the women, when they look at the plants they look at the firewood. They chop everything down. So what is important to children is to teach them about indigenous stuff, that they must look after it… because once we lose it we don’t have any.
VO
Benny’s love for the environment comes from his grandmother, and she was the one who first introduced him to the fossils on the beach, just a few kilometres south of the village.
Benny
She told me a lot, and she used to even shout at people that were breaking up the fossils on the beach, when I go with her to the beach.
UPS
Bye… see you after work!
VO
Today’s “work” – for Benny – is taking us on a tour of the fossils along the coast… But because we need to wait for low tide to explore the shore properly… Benny takes us on a bit of a sidequest.
Benny
Benny: They’re called Mzamba fossils because of this river.

Claire: This river that we are seeing now? This is the Mzamba river?

Benny: Yeah.

Claire: Okay


VO
Benny has many happy memories of this place…
Benny
We used to bring the cattle down there and we know they are not going to go out. We play around and we fish around and later on in the afternoon we fetch them back home…
VO
And if this gorge looks somewhat familiar, it’s because you’ve probably seen it in one of the many productions that have been filmed here over the last decade…
Benny
Starting from Blood Diamond, Man to Man, Survivor… and lots and lots… And the last one to be filmed here was iLelmbe; Shaka Zulu.

Claire: are you saying we’re standing where Leonardo Di Caprio was standing?

Benny: yeah.

Claire: I love you Benny for bringing me here. Thank you.
VO
It’s just after one when we make our way to the beach where the Mzamba river meets the ocean…
Benny
From this river we’re walking straight to the fossils.
VO
It’s hot, and this morning’s breeze has turned into a gusty north-easterly… ,
UPS
Claire: Well I must say I like your office, this is a good office to have, Benny.

Benny: Yeah, I always dream about my little office…
VO
Benny points out one of the first fossils discovered in 1824…
Benny
Benny: Looks exactly like a rock, but when you take a nice look you can see where the tree trunk is.

Claire: yes!
VO
This entire stretch of beach is dotted with the remains of trees from Central African forests that washed down the rivers and were eventually fossilised here…

They date back to a time known as the Late Cretaceous Epoch… an era that lasted around 34 million years. Sea levels were over 200 metres higher than today, and the continents were flooded with marine waters…
VO




Shelled cephalopods, distant relatives of modern-day squid and octopi – known as ammonites – lived in the shallow oceans …

Their fossilized shells are found across the world, even here at Mzamba beach.
UPS
Benny: Look at this baby ammonite.

Claire: I can see! Oh my gosh.
VO
Ancient seas were once teeming with these marine predators
UPS
Benny: That one is not very big…
VO
and scientists have identified over 10,000 species of varying shapes and sizes…

Many of the bigger ammonites are buried under the sand as the landscape here is changing…
UPS
Benny: I think it’s all about the sand eroding from inland.

Claire: I was just about to say, is it a bigger issue?

Ja, it’s because the land eroding has become a great issue, more specially far inland.
VO
The siltation of rivers means that a lot more sand ends up on the beach… but Benny is prepared to dig… even in this wind!
UPS
Benny: As soon as I open it, you’ll view it because the wind is going to cover it up again.

Claire: Okay
VO
These ocean-dwelling molluscs became extinct along with the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago.
Benny
The ammonites are one of the very important index fossils that help the scientists determine the rock age.
UPS
Claire: How big is it?

Benny: Bigger than the other one.

Claire: Yeah
VO
Because ammonites are abundant and widespread, they can help to date other fossils found in the same marine rock layers.
Benny
Here you go


Claire: It is big!

Benny: it starts from here… it goes all the way to here…

Claire: WOW


VO
After little more than an hour on the beach we are fully sandblasted… but Benny has the perfect spot for us to escape the wind for a bit…
UPS
Claire, welcome to the Mzamba caves…
VO
These might look like ordinary beach caves, but if you know what to look for, they too tell a story of a forgotten time…
UPS
Benny: You can see the white marks or lines… those are the clam shells.The rest of it was broken out, but the rest of it is still inside.
VO
These clams were several meters in diameter. And right next to them… a fossilised sea turtle.
UPS
This is the tail side, and the rest of the turtle… then you can see the head squashed on the wall with the eye socket.
VO
Over the past 50 years Benny has seen many changes here…
UPS
You can see the roof of the cave is made out of fossils. And then here somebody was trying to steal my ammonite… and he failed to take them out.
VO
Even though this is a protected area and a natural heritage site, unscrupulous visitors still remove fossils illegally… and it’s impossible for Benny to guard them full time.
UPS
Benny: When maybe I die I would like to be buried here on top of the caves here. So then I can look after these caves 24 hours…

Claire: Even in the afterlife.

Benny: Yeah.




Benny
To me, being a tourist guide is all about making sure all the beautiful things that God gave to us… we will keep them forever.
Link
The sun is setting, the tide is coming in and pretty soon our footprints will be washed away… I wonder what other treasures lie here hidden beneath the sand and waves…








PROMO 1 21”
A unique series of fossil beds along the Wild Coast…

UPS: it’s very rare to find fossils on the beach around the world…

And one man’s passion to preserve them for future generations…



PROMO 2 21”
In Pondoland Benny Mboto is a bit of a legend…

MUSIC

He’s a musician and electrician, but his real passion is safeguarding a one-of-a-kind fossil collection along the Wild Coast shoreline…


PROMO 3 21”
A story of a man with a passion for the natural heritage of the Wild Coast…



We meet Benny Mboto, The guardian of the Mzamba fossils.
